title: Saag Aloo
subtitle: Indian spinach and potato curry
excerpt: Saag aloo is a simple North Indian dry curry of spiced potatoes and spinach. It comes together in under 30 minutes and works as a side or a main with rice or flatbread. The combination of whole and ground spices gives it good depth without long cooking.
sourceNotes: Saag aloo is a staple of North Indian home cooking, particularly in Punjab. Saag refers to leafy greens -- traditionally mustard leaves -- though spinach is now the most common version outside of the subcontinent.

content.text: Cut the potatoes into even 2cm cubes so they cook at the same rate. Frozen spinach works well here -- thaw it fully and squeeze out the excess water before adding, or the curry will be watery.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and fry for 30 seconds until they begin to sizzle and smell fragrant.
Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes, stirring regularly, until golden and soft.
Stir in the garlic and ginger. Cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell fades.
Add the turmeric and coriander. Stir for 1 minute to coat the onions.
Add the potato cubes and tinned tomatoes. Pour in 150ml of water. Season with salt. Cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes, stirring halfway, until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the spinach and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until heated through and any excess liquid evaporates.
Sprinkle over the garam masala. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with basmati rice or flatbread.

items.cause: The cubes may be too large, or the heat too low
items.fix: Add a splash more water, cover tightly, and cook for another 5 minutes

items.cause: Spinach was not squeezed dry before adding
items.fix: Remove the lid and cook on medium heat, stirring, until the excess liquid evaporates

items.cause: Ground spices were added without enough frying time
items.fix: Next time, fry the ground spices for a full minute before adding the potatoes

content.text: Saag aloo is everyday home food across North India and Pakistan. In Punjab, it is often made with mustard greens rather than spinach. Restaurants tend to add cream, but the home version is lighter and drier. It sits well alongside dal or as part of a larger spread.
